html:
Sugar plantations ruled the economy of Hawaii for more than a century, from the first commercial plantation at Kōloa on Kauaʻi in 1835 until the last mill closed in 2016.

Planters, many of them sons of American missionaries, needed land and labour. The Great Māhele let them buy land, and they brought in workers from China, Japan, Portugal, Korea and the Philippines. These labourers are why Hawaii has its unusually mixed population; see Japanese migration.

Sugar tied Hawaii to the American market. Planters wanted duty-free sales, and their political power led directly to the overthrow of the monarchy in 1893 and annexation by the United States.
sum: Sugar plantations ruled the economy of Hawaii for more than a century, from the first commercial plantation at Kōloa on Kauaʻi in 1835 until the last mill closed in 2016.
